doc.title: Chazz Frichtel interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, June 13, 2016

title: Debt to Central New York musicians and Dick Robilatto
summary: Frichtel credits his high school band director Dick Robilatto and the Central New York community, and Rowe recalls learning from local players.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Learning your horn: teachers, lessons and fees

blocks.x: Oh man, I can’t tell you how much Dick Robilatto, what kind of influence he had on my life. And I was lucky enough that I got him on the phone not too long before he passed away. I’m not even sure he knew for certain who he was talking to. But he said, “Yeah I had a student Charlie who went out to L.A. I think he’s doing okay out there.” And it was just so touching. He was my high school band director. He was such a wonderful guy. But that’s, you know I have said time and time again I feel such a debt to the musicians in Central New York. There’s such a rich musical heritage that comes from this area. And many, many great players come from here and I feel lucky to have really grown up here, and I feel that the community here enabled me to go and swim in the L.A. pond. And I’m telling you this now, I’ve told Carmen [Caramanica], I’ve told Ricky [Montalbano], if I could tell Sal Amico I would tell him, Chick, Chick knew. Chick — we got together in L.A. one time. He took a trip to L.A. and it was really, really great to see him. Really great to see him.

I’ve told Rick and Carmen that too. Because when I first moved up here I managed to get a gig with the both of them and Dolores Mancuso at the Beeches. And I just sat on my stool with my sax and I watched and listened to what they did. And I thought I knew a lot because I had gone to music school. But I didn’t know anything about playing gigs and filling what people’s expectations would be, or beyond. It was really an education for me.
